title: Six leaks
hookLine: wealth drains through drink, night-roaming, fairs, gambling, bad company and idleness
carry: too hot, too late, too tired

cards: Open a banking app and look at last month. There's usually no single disaster. Just a lot of small drips: a subscription you forgot, takeout three nights running, a late-night purchase you can't quite remember making.
The money didn't explode. It leaked. The Buddha, talking to a young householder in a world with no apps, names the same thing: six openings through which a household's wealth drains away.

teach.b: The Pali word is apayamukha, literally a mouth or opening toward loss. The six: drinking intoxicants, roaming the streets at the wrong hours, haunting fairs and shows, gambling, keeping bad company, and idleness.
For each one, the Buddha lists six dangers, and the details are wonderfully specific.

Gambling: the winner makes enemies, the loser mourns what he lost, his money is gone, his word isn't trusted when he speaks in public, his friends look down on him, and nobody wants him to marry into their family.
Roaming at night: he leaves himself unprotected, and his family and property too, he's suspected of crimes, and rumors attach to him. And idleness has the best list of all.

teach.h: TOO COLD, TOO HOT, TOO LATE.
teach.b: The idle man doesn't work, saying: it's too cold. It's too hot. It's too late.
It's too early. I'm too hungry. I'm too full.
Every reason sounds reasonable. That's what makes it a leak.
This isn't a sermon against pleasure, and he isn't asking a householder to live like a monk. Elsewhere in the same sutta he tells him to enjoy part of his wealth.
He's simply pointing to where it goes when you're not watching.
And the leaks aren't only money. Each one drains time, health, trust and friendships too. None of them is dramatic.
It's one more drink, one more night out, one more too late, too early.

how: Buddhist teachers often teach the Sigalovada's six leaks to lay people as practical household advice, and Buddhist economics writers cite it alongside the sutta's advice on saving and sharing wealth.

o: six habits that drain a household's wealth
six taxes a king took from his people

p: too cold, too hot, too late

s: the Buddha tells Sigala to give up all pleasure
the same sutta tells him to enjoy part of his wealth; the leaks are about where it drains.
each leak in DN 31 comes with six dangers
six openings, each with its own list of six.
among the idle man's excuses is 'I'm too full'
too cold, too hot, too late, too early, too hungry, too full.

games.q: it's a hot afternoon and there's work to do. the idle man in the Sigalovada has an answer ready. what is it?
o: I'll do twice as much tomorrow.
games.why: it's too hot, and if it isn't, it's too cold, too late, too early, too hungry or too full.

practice: Look honestly at your own week, without blame, and ask where something leaks: money, yes, but also time, energy, attention.
Let the most ordinary leak come to mind, and picture the moment it usually happens: the evening, the phone, the excuse. Breathe with it, and picture plugging it, just once.

wordCard.voice: Six leaks. In DN 31 the six openings through which wealth drains: drink, night-roaming, fairs, gambling, bad company and idleness. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali apayamukha: apaya, loss or ruin; mukha, mouth or opening. the six leaks of DN 31.

carryVoice: Your line: too hot, too late, too tired. Small drips, not disasters. Day five hundred sixty-eight.
